viii PREFACE The Moyers Symposium occupies a unique and distinguished place within the orthodontic and craniofacial biology community, serving as a cornerstone for scientific exchange and the advancement of clinical practice. Each year, this symposium draws together practitioners, researchers, educators, and students, united by a commitment to both the heritage and the forward momentum of the field. The Fifty-second Annual Moyers Symposium, held in Ann Arbor on March 1-2, 2025, continues this tradition, presenting a program purposefully centered on "Back to Basics." Amid a landscape inundated with enthusiasm and rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and technology, this meeting aims to connect the foundational principles of orthodontics with the latest research and contemporary clinical practice. It offers a thoughtful integration of proven methods and new discoveries, all anchored by scientific inquiry and a spirit of collegiality. In doing so, we reafﬁrm our dedication to

clinical practice. It offers a thoughtful integration of proven methods and new discoveries, all anchored by scientific inquiry and a spirit of collegiality. In doing so, we reafﬁrm our dedication to evidence-based, patient-centered care. As with tradition, the Symposium is preceded by the Annual International Conference on Craniofacial Research, known affectionately as "The Presymposium". This interdisciplinary gathering of researchers from all over the world further enriches the conversations and collaborations that the Moyers Symposium inspires. Our invited speakers represent a broad spectrum of expertise, spanning clinical practice, research, and ethics. This year’s discussions encompass historical perspectives and ethics, the critical importance of timing and prediction in growth and development, biomechanics, material science, retention and stability, current best practices in diagnostic imaging, and the prevention and management of orthodontic complications. ORTHODONTIC ESSENTIALS: OUR IDENTITY , OUR LIBERTY Peter M. Greco ABSTRACT Th e future of orthodontics as an autonomous specialty is vastly dependent on our professional image. We must maintain a standard of behavior hallmarked by integrity, respect for our proud legacy, an expanding but evidence-based knowledge base, and innovation that beneﬁts our patient s as well as ourselves. We need to demonstrate a century old but fully applicable objective “to combine the old morality with the new economy.” KEY WOR DS: Liberty, Professionalism, Legacy INTRODUCTION A mong the essentials of earning the title of orthodontist are skills and virtues that are less tangib le than those such as bending a closing loop arch wire, placing a bracket ideally, or treatment planning for a complex Class III malocclusion. Equally as important are the ethical and professional attributes that earn us the status of becoming worthy of the title of professional: such are the nuts and bolts of our image. These

These essentials will strongly inﬂuence the way we practice —and deﬁne our liberty as specialists —for decades to come. Lib erty is deﬁned as the power and scope to act as one pleases . Philadelphians feel a special connection to liberty, as freedom is historically ingrained in our culture. Thomas Jeﬀerson and our nation’s forefathers deﬁned liberty in their Declaration of Independence here in 1776. Liberty remains an essential political concept, yet liberty is also important to what we do as healers and in deﬁning us as professionals. A s orthodontists in a changing climate of professional identity, we must ask ourselves how we can individually or collectively maintain the liberty to practice orthodontics as we please in the future. ntity, we must ask ourselves how we can individually or collectively maintain the liberty to practice orthodontics as we please in the future. In other words, each of us must ask ourselves, “How can I keep this specialty special?” T o answer that question, let’s look at the liberty of our cousins, the physicians. There are those among that profession who consider their liberty jeopardized. Dr. Stephen Furr deﬁnes the challenge to physicians’ liberty by a number of factors , including government interference, constraints on referral patterns, declining insurance authorization and reimbursement , healthcare regulations, patient quotas imposed by hospitals and corporations that employ them, and time constraints potentially leading to practitioner burnout [1]. Wh at liberties do we —orthodontists—need to preserve our independence ? There are several. We need independence from the inﬂuence of insurance companies. We need to maintain our individuality as a specialty without becoming

rthodontists—need to preserve our independence ? There are several. We need independence from the inﬂuence of insurance companies. We need to maintain our individuality as a specialty without becoming absorbed by other disciplines. We need to remain as the source for orthodontics and dentofacial orthopedics. We need to uphold our administrative autonomy. We need to maintain our image of professionalism by focusing on quality patient care rather than quotas. Orthodontic Essentials Greco 1

A lmost one hundred years ago the eminent Canadian physician Dr. Earl P Scarlett (1886-1982) admonished the medical profession as follows: “If we of the profession are to answer the challenge of our time successfully, we must somehow manage to combine the old morality with the new economy .” (Emphasis added) [2]. Wh at are the challenges of our time ? A ccording to a 2015 letter written by the A A O t o i t s membership, the challenges include the following : a decrease in restorative needs , an in crease in the number of orthodontic graduates with debt, an increase in non-orthodontists providing orthodontic care, an increase in competitive marketing, an increase in deceptive advertising, an increase in do -it-yourself treatment, and an increase in the use of social media to promote treatment that is often not evidence based [3]. KEY WORD S: Impacted canine, Biomechanics, Force system, Anchorage control INTRODUCTION Canine impaction is a challenging clinical situation for the orthodontist today. Maxillary impacted canines are observed in about 2% of the population and impaction of mandibular canines is rare compared to maxillary ones (0.35%) [1-3]. Most impaction of canines occurs in the palate (85%) and only 15% on the labial aspect of the maxilla [2, 3]. Girls are twice as likely to be more aﬀected as boys. Impacted canines are bilateral in 8% of cases and they are ﬁve times more common in Caucasians than in Asians [2]. Clinically, a lack of space on the arch is associated with labially impacted canines, whereas, palatally impacted canines generally have adequate space to erupt [2, 4]. The treatment planning of these cases is complex, and the appropriate biomechanics need to be considered based on the correct diagnosis and treatment goals. The timing and accuracy of the diagnosis are critical factors that may help avoid the impaction of canines in some situations. Regular dental appointment s and follow up of the sequence of eruption are necessary in children starting at an early age. This allows for the early imaging of the maxillary canines and helps in determining the prognosis of a successful eruption of the maxillary canine. The orthodontist must consider the information obtained from the clinical and 3D analysis and incorporate it in a list of detailed treatment goals. This allows the clinician to develop various treatment options and consider several plans if necessary. Some of the questions that need to be addressed during this phase include the following: • W here is the canine located with respect to surrounding teeth and how severe is the impaction? Is the root of the canine in a favorable position to be erupted on the arch? T he clinical presentation and the outcomes are diﬀerent for palatally and labially impacted canines. On the palatal aspect, the canines have enough attached gingiva, and the question is often whether to proceed with an open or closed exposure. I n light of the evidence available in the current literature, the clinician plays a critical role in discussing the type of canine exposure with the oral surgeon or periodontist. It is therefore crucial that our approach to retention is evidence -based. Evidence -based retention means integrating research evidence, clinical expertise, and patient values. Ranking the quality of research evidence determines how conﬁdent we can be in the results of diﬀerent types of retainer research. The ﬁndings of the most recent Cochrane review into retention procedures provides useful information about various types of ﬁxed and removable retainers, and how often to wear removable retainers. The long-term success of retainers depends on patients being willing, able, and motivated to continue to wear, care for, and maintain their retainers. This ensures that the review process is transparent and can be replicated by others. Ther e is a recognized scientiﬁc approach to undertaking a systematic review: • identify a speciﬁc and clearly deﬁned question • use thorough and transparent search strategies to identify all relevant studies • critically appraise the studies for their quality and reliability • synthesize the ﬁndings of included studies to draw conclusions about the overall evidence on the research question. While orthodontic appliances are often blamed for WSL development, extended plaque retention due to inadequate or al hygiene is the main cause of demineralization. The appearance of white spots on the facial surfaces of teeth at the end of orthodontic treatment can lead to unsatisfactory treatment outcomes and patient dissatisfaction. Thus, grasping these key concepts is essential for clinicians to assist patients in maintaining proper oral hygiene during orthodontic treatment and effectively managing their cases. WSLs appear as opaque, white areas on the buccal surfaces of teeth and can significantly affect the esthetic outcomes of orthodontic treatment. In orthodontic patients, particularly those with fixed appliances, the oral environment is subject to fluctuations in salivary pH, which can influence the equilibrium between enamel demineralization and remineralization. This equilibrium can shift depending on various factors, such as diet, oral hygiene, and orthodontic appliances [19]. After consuming fermentable carbohydrates, oral bacteria metabolize these sugars, producing acids that lower the pH in dental plaque. However, the buffering effect of saliva, due to bicarbonate ions, helps neutralize acids and restore pH levels [21]. An increase in salivary flow rate, often observed during orthodontic treatment, is believed to enhance the buffering effect and facilitate the dilution of acid. PANORAMIC RADIOGRAPHS Panoramic radiographs are among the most commonly used extraoral imaging modalities in dentistry. They provide a broad overview of the maxillofacial region, including the teeth, jaws, temporomandibular joints (TMJs), and adjacent structures. Despite being a 2D representation of complex 3D anatomy, panoramic radiography remains a valuable tool for initial evaluation, treatment planning, and detecting abnormalities. A systematic, region-based approach ensures a comprehensive review, minimizing the risk of missing critical ﬁndings. 1. Indications Panoramic radiographs are indicated in a wide variety of clinical contexts. They are often used for initial orthodontic records and assessment, third molar evaluation, and dental age estimation and eruption

mic radiographs are indicated in a wide variety of clinical contexts. They are often used for initial orthodontic records and assessment, third molar evaluation, and dental age estimation and eruption patterns. Clinicians also utilize them for the detection of osseous pathology like cysts, tumors, or infections, and for the evaluation of trauma. While their use is limited, they can also assist in pre mini-implant assessment, TMJ screening, foreign body localization, and preliminary sinus evaluation. A lthough panoramic images have limitations in resolution and dimensional accuracy, they remain a ﬁrst-line imaging modality due to their low radiation dose, broad coverage, and quick acquisition time [5]. 2. Image characteristics Structures Flattened and Spread Out Panoramic radiographs project 3D structures onto a 2D image, where the buccolingual dimension is compressed, making it impossible to assess bone thickness and spatial relationships. Because of the curvilinear nature of the focal trough, some structures —especially those located along the curve of the dental arches—may appear ﬂattened, distorted, or spread out. This distortion can aﬀect structures such as the inferior nasal turbinates , which are anatomically located in the nasal cavity but spread out and superimposed onto the maxillary sinuses, making it diﬃcult to determine if the sinuses are clear. Similarly, the hard palate may be superimposed on the roots of maxillary teeth if the chin is positioned too high during image acquisition. Single and Double Images Panoramic radiography can produce either single or double images based on how the x-ray beam interacts with midline and bilateral structures. Single images are created when a structure lies within the path of the beam and is imaged only once, which

or double images based on how the x-ray beam interacts with midline and bilateral structures. Single images are created when a structure lies within the path of the beam and is imaged only once, which is typical in the case of the teeth and sinuses. Double images, however, occur when midline structures such as the soft palate, hyoid bone, epiglottis, or cervical spine are intercepted twice by the x-ray beam as it rotates, creating mirror-like duplicates. Some of these double images can be superimposed with the other anatomical structures, partially obscuring their visualization. For example, the double real images of the soft palate are partially superimposed with the rami, and the hyoid bone can be superimposed with the body of the mandible if the patient swallows during the scan. Real and Ghost Images Understanding the diﬀerence between real and ghost images is crucial for accurate interpretation. Real images are formed by structures located between the rotation center and the sensor . In contrast, ghost images occur when structures and objects, such as the mandible or earrings, lie between the x-ray source and the rotation center but outside the focal trough. These ghost images appear on the opposite side of the image from the real object, are typically projected higher up, and appear more magniﬁed, blurry, and closer to the midline . They are often seen with metallic accessories such as jewelry, hearing aids, or orthodontic bands. Clinically, ghost images can obscure anatomical structures and may compromise the diagnostic quality of the radiograph to the point that a retake may be necessary. Soft Tissues and Cartilages Although the hard tissues are the primary focus of panoramic radiograph y, some of the soft tissues and cartilages can also be visualized. These include the nasal and alar cartilage, the soft palate and uvula, the tongue (which can cause a palatoglossal air space if not pressed against the palate), and the ear lobe and tragus. Overlapping soft tissues, such as the soft palate and the ala of the nose, can sometimes mimic lesions as they increase the degree of radiopacity of the area where they are superimposed. Air Spaces Panoramic radiographs capture various air-ﬁlled spaces that appear radiolucent. Common air spaces include the palatoglossal air space (between the tongue and hard palate), the nasopharyngeal air space (behind the nasal cavity), the oropharyngeal air space (posterior to the oral cavity), and the glossopharyngeal air space (behind the tongue and pharynx). They typically appear as well-demarcated radiolucencies and are usually symmetrical unless pathology is present , the head position is rotated , or there are swallowing artifacts Of these air spaces, the palatoglossal air space is considered a technical error that may obscure maxillary root apices. To avoid it, p atients should always be instructed to press their tongue against the palate during exposure, which eliminates this air space and improves image quality. 3. Technical considerations Correct patient positioning is critical for acquiring a diagnostic quality panoramic radiograph (Figure 1). Key positioning criteria include ensuring the Frankfort plane is parallel to the ﬂoor, the midsagittal plane is aligned with the midline positioning light , and the tongue is pressed against the palate to avoid the palatoglossal air

ensuring the Frankfort plane is parallel to the ﬂoor, the midsagittal plane is aligned with the midline positioning light , and the tongue is pressed against the palate to avoid the palatoglossal air space. Additionally, teeth should be positioned within the focal trough according to the manufacturer’s guidelines. Mispositioning can lead to distortions that may mimic pathology or obscure anatomy. Common errors include placing the teeth too far anteriorly or posteriorly with respect to the focal trough, where anterior teeth appear wider (if placed too far back ) or narrower (if placed too far forward) than normal. If the chin is tipped down excessively, an exaggerated smile line and distortion of the mandibular anterior region may occur. 5. Common pathologies detected on panoramic radiographs P anoramic radiographs are useful for detecting various common pathologies. These include odontogenic cysts (e.g., dentigerous cysts, radicular cysts), benign tumors (e.g., ameloblastoma, odontoma), and though far less common, primary or metastatic malignant lesions. Image quality and technical considerations Before beginning any analysis, it is essential to ensure that the image is of diagnostic quality. The patient should be positioned in a natural head posture, with the teeth in centric occlusion unless otherwise specified. Machine model design: data normalization and validation Given the semi-longitudinal nature of the available data and the relative paucity of the sample, it was necessary to use all available time intervals. The model was trained to predict the evolution of the coordinates for all time -ordered observations of an y given patient. Moreover, a small Gaussian noise was added to both training and test cephalometric points. For this reason, the X and Y coordinates in model output were an average of 10 predictions taken from 10 noise realizations. Normalization of coordinate values To normalize the coordinates, all 16 cephalometric points were set in a Cartesian axis with points X and Y for each cephalometric point (Figure 1). The X-axis was represented as a line passing through Nasion (N) with an angulation of 7° upwards with respect to the SN line, while the Y-axis was defined as a line perpendicular to X -axis and passing though Sella point. Algorithm training and testing To develop the predictive model, the sample was divided randomly into two groups: a training group and a testing group. The training group consisted of 80% of the subjects, selected randomly, while the remaining 20% constituted the test group. This distribution resulted in a training group comprising 116 subjects and a testing group comprising 28 subjects. The trained model was a graph neural network (GNN) consisting of one graph convolution layer (https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.029) [28] and one fully connected layer for prediction. GNNs capture graph dependencies via message passing between nodes [34], mimicking the way neurons in the human brain process information to identify patterns and reach conclusions [35]. The model was tested for both short-term predictions (within 1.5 years from T0) and long-term predictions (more than 3 years from T0). This fully automated protocol was applied to a sample of 17 skeletal Class III patients. After surgery, most patients showed minimal condylar remodeling (<1 mm) across the overall surface and individual poles. Bone resorption predominantly occurred at the superior articular surface, while bone apposition was mainly observed at the lateral pole (Figure 10). Patterns of condylar displacement included medial, posterior, and inferior shifts on both sides. Signiﬁcant correlations were found between regional bon e remodeling and condylar displacement, highlighting distinct remodeling behaviors at speciﬁc condylar regions following surgery. Patients were treated with rapid maxillary expansion (RME) and facemask therapy (FM). The ﬁrst trial involved 10 subjects with Class III malocclusions who were treated with a RME and a Petit-type FM. This syndrome is particularly concerning because it often encompasses multiple risk factors such as abdominal obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidemia (elevated cholesterol levels), and hyperglycemia (high blood sugar levels). The presence of these risk factors not only increases individual health risks but also places a signiﬁcant burden on healthcare systems. Various studies have shown that those with metabolic syndrome are at a substantially greater risk for cardiovascular events and other health complications. Implementing lifestyle modiﬁcations—such as balanced healthy diets, exercise, stress management, and body weight control—can eﬀectively reduce the risk of developing more serious health issues linked to metabolic syndrome. alth, Salivary glands, Sjorgren’s disease, Orthodontics INTRODUCTION Metabolic diseases represent a signiﬁcant and escalating health issue, not only within the United States but also on a global scale [1-3]. These conditions are frequently associated with severe health complications, including heart disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, dementia, speciﬁc types of cancer, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease [4-7]. While the relationships between metabolic disorders and these health concerns are well established, it is imperative to emphasize some of the lesser -known risks associated with these disorders, such as the potential for birth defects, various bone diseases, and dry mouth, all of which can substa ntially impact oral health and the outcome of orthodontic treatment. A comprehensive understanding of these risks is essential for the maintenance of optimal bone and oral health, as they are integral to overall well-being and the eﬃcacy of orthodontic treatments. For example, compromised bone health may complicate orthodontic procedures by hindering the proper anchoring of teeth. Dry mouth, which may arise from metabolic disorders or the side eﬀects of certain medications, can create a favorable environ ment for caries and periodontal disease s [8, 9] , thus complicating dental treatments and potentially leading to detrimental outcomes. In light of these risks, it is vital to educate and raise awareness among healthcare professionals, dental practitioners, and researchers regarding the intricate interplay between metabolic diseases and oral health. In particular, there is a speciﬁc relationship between cholesterol metabolism abnormalities and their eﬀects on bone and saliva production. Current research suggests that alterations in cholesterol metabolism can lead to decreased bone density and increase the risk of osteoporosis and fractures [10- 13] attributed to impaired osteoblast functions [14, 15], which are critical for bone repair and regeneration. Additionally, abnormal cholesterol levels may aﬀect the production and composition of saliva, diminishing its protective properties against dental caries and periodontal disease s, essential factors for maintaining oral health. Eﬀective management of metabolic diseases can be a safeguard of oral health and successful orthodontic outcomes. This chapter aims to highlight the importance of cholesterol metabolism in oral health, as a lesson from animal studies. BONES IN CHOLESTEROL METABOLISM ABNORMALITIES Nearly every cell within the human body is equipped with the primary cilium, a specialized cell surface structure that functions analogously to a cellular antenna [16]. This organelle is instrumental in the coordination of various cellular signaling pathways, the sensations of extracellular cues, and the execution of signal transduction processes [16]. The primary cilia play a critical role in osteoblast proliferation , osteogenic diﬀerentiation, and the maintenance of bone homeostasis [17-19]. Cholesterol, an essential lipid component of cellular membranes, is integral to the structural integrity and functional eﬃcacy of primary cilia [20, 21]. It contributes to the maintenance of membrane ﬂuidity, thereby facilitating eﬀective protein traﬃcking [22, 23] . Furthermore, cholesterol is essential for the formation of lipid rafts and caveolae —distinct microdomains

e maintenance of membrane ﬂuidity, thereby facilitating eﬀective protein traﬃcking [22, 23] . Furthermore, cholesterol is essential for the formation of lipid rafts and caveolae —distinct microdomains within the membrane that serve as organizational hubs for the assembly and interaction of signaling molecules [22, 23]. These microdomains are vital in initiating and regulating signal transduction events. Additionally, cholesterol becomes a source of several important biomolecules such as steroid hormones, oxysterols, and bile acids, emphasizing its multifaceted role in the body [24]. This cholesterol enrichment within primary cilia further underscores its critical importance in their structural dynamics. The synthesis of cholesterol is a multifaceted biochemical process involving numerous enzymatic reactions [25]. Within these glands, acinar cells are instrumental in synthesizing and secreting salivary proteins, which are functional constituents of saliva [30-32]. This secretion process occurs via exocytosis, which includes the processes of the transport of vesicles ﬁlled with salivary proteins to the cellular membrane, the fusion of these vesicles with the plasma membrane, and the release of their contents into the salivary ducts [33, 34]. NEURAL PATHWAYS CONTROLLING THE MASTICATORY MUSCLES IN OROFACIAL FUNCTION AND DYSFUNCTION Karin Harumi Uchima Koecklin, Peng Li ABSTRACT O rofacial functions including chewing, swallowing, breathing, and vocalization rely on precise jaw movements. Disturbances in these functions such as masticatory dysfunction and bruxism can lead to severe consequences including malocclusion, muscle pain, and temporomandibular disorders. Jaw movements are governed by the coordinated activity of the masticatory muscles innervated by the trigeminal nerve. Sensory feedback, particularly proprioception, which is the body’s ability to sense the position and movem ent, plays a critical role in modulating motor control. In the orofacial area, proprioceptive information is processed by the mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve (Vmes), a unique structure located in the brainstem. The Vmes receives the proprioceptive information from diﬀerent orofacial structures including the masticatory muscles, periodontal ligament, and temporomandibular joint (TMJ). Alterations in the proprioceptive signaling and processing can lead to disruption in the motor control of the masticatory muscles, aﬀecting the orofacial functions. Emerging evidence suggests that Vmes-mediated proprioception is essential not only for normal orofacial functions, particularly chewing, but also in the pathogenesis of related disorders. The aim of this chapter is to highlight the critical role of proprioception in both normal orofacial functions and dysfunction, providing key insights for achieving optimal functional outcomes. These complex behaviors depend on precise neuromuscular coordination to prevent airway obstruction [1]. S uccessful execution of these functions requires controlled jaw movements, with coordinated activity of the masticatory muscles [2-4]. Understanding the neural pathways involved in the control of the orofacial functions and disturbances requires the study of the sensory feedback and how this modulates the motor response [1]. Within the masticatory muscles, the masseter muscle is crucial for the skeletal shaping, as it is involved in the etiology of some malocclusion problems, but also provides occlusal stability after orthodontic treatment [16]. T he execution of orofacial functions , such as chewing and swallowing, requires precise control and coordination. These actions depend not only on the jaw-opening and jaw-closing muscles, but also other orofacial muscles innervated by ﬁve cranial nerves [17]. The trigeminal nerve presents one motor nucleus, located in the pons, and three sensory nuclei: the principal, the spinal, and the Vmes, which are distributed along the brainstem [25]. T he motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve (Vmotor) provides motor innervation to the jaw opening muscles, including the anterior belly of the digastric, mylohyoid, and lateral pterygoid, and the jaw-closing muscles including the masseter, temporalis, and medial pterygoid, as well as the tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini [10, 11, 25, 26]. The motor nucleus is anatomically organized into two distinct compartments, a dorsolateral and a ventromedial region. The dorsolateral region primarily innervates to the jaw closing muscles including the masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid, and jaw-opening lateral pterygoid. T he primary sensory neurons in the orofacial area are distributed across both the peripheral and central compartments: the trigeminal ganglia and the Vmes. While most of these sensory neurons reside peripherally in the trigeminal ganglia, a distinct subset is located within the Vmes, representing a specialized feature of the trigeminal sensory system [27]. The sensory information from the trigeminal ganglia is relayed by the principal and spinal trigeminal nuclei located in the brainstem . These nuclei process the general sensation, including, touch, temperature, and pain from the orofacial area. On the other hand, the Vmes receives the sensory information directly from the orofacial area for proprioception [25, 26]. Th e role of the mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve (Vmes) in oral proprioception Th e Vmes, housing large primary sensory neurons [14] between the rostral pons and the midbrain, contains the only ﬁrst order neurons in the central nervous system in vertebrates [28, 29]. This unique anatomy facilitates both orofacial proprioception, functionally equivalent to the proprioceptive neurons in the dorsal root ganglia [30], and integration of the peripheral signals with the inputs from other central regions [31]. B esides the uniqueness of the location of these neurons, they also have a distinctive embryonic origin, as they are derived from the neuroepithelium located in the dorsal midline of the midbrain, as opposed to other primary sensory neurons that originate from the neural crest cells or neurogenic placodes [32]. Benton Swanson, Katherine Kelly, Yuji Mishina, Justine Moe AB STRACT C raniosynostosis is the premature fusion of cranial bones due to premature loss of specific cell populations within the cranial suture, which lies between developing cranial bones. Recent evidence demonstrates that polymer scaffolds with pores of sufficiently small size (<125 um) can control cell fate and maintain stemness. In this study, a method for testing such biomaterial scaffolds was developed for the purpose of investigating craniofacial applications. Initial attempts included surgical removal of the sagittal or coronal suture. Limitations of these methods led to a surgical protocol described herein as the “artificial suture protocol” because a surgical procedure for creating a rectangular defect within the parietal bone of 3-week-old mice was created, to

d to a surgical protocol described herein as the “artificial suture protocol” because a surgical procedure for creating a rectangular defect within the parietal bone of 3-week-old mice was created, to determine if polymer scaffolds of small pore size could lead this surgical defect to function much like a cranial suture in terms of preventing mineralization, promoting cell stemness, and promoting cranial bone growth in a dire ction perpendicular to the suture. The primary goals of this study were to optimize a surgical protocol for scaffold placement in terms of consistent and replicable bone removal in the surgical defect site without impacting brain function and maintaining mouse health immediately post-surgery and over time. K EY WORDS: Craniosynostosis, Suture, Biomaterial, Scaffold, Surgery INTRODUCTION D uring human growth and development, the immature calvaria begins its formation with the growth of five key bones. These five bones are the frontal and parietal bones (each of which are a pair of two bones) and the occipital bone [1]. Unlike many of the long bones of the human skeleton , which form via a process known as endochondral ossification, the cranial bones mature through the process of intramembranous ossification, whereby osteoblasts differentiate directly from mesenchymal cells [2]. Intramembranous bone formation begins as dense regions of mesenchymal cells begin to proliferate until a critical mass is reached. Once this occurs, the mesenchymal cells in the center of the growing cell population begin to

Once this occurs, the mesenchymal cells in the center of the growing cell population begin to mature into osteoblasts. Eventually, the outer edge of the growing bones forms an osteogenic front. When growing cranial bones come into proximity with each other, a cranial suture is formed between the two adjacent osteogenic fronts. This suture tissue contains intermediate suture mesenchyme that is not mineralized and provides stem and osteoprogenitor cells needed for continued cranial bone growth [2, 3]. The establishment of cranial sutures occurs at approximately 18 weeks of prenatal development [4]. A cranial suture is defined as the mesenchymal soft tissue that lies in between the developing bones of the cranium [5]. The process of cranial growth occurs through an appositional mechanism whereby osteoid (pre -mineralized bony matrix) is deposited at suture margins [4]. It has been shown that, depending on the location of mesenchymal cells within the developing cranial suture, certain cells differentiate and certain cells do not. Those cells that differentiate into osteoblasts and become incorporated into the developing cranial bones are located at the edge of the suture, adjacent to osteogenic fronts [2]. In contrast, suture cells that are located within the middle of the suture remain undifferentiated, thereby preserving suture patency and a source of stem/progenitor cells. It is hypothesized that conditions such as craniosynostosis result s from an imbalance in the recruitment of suture mesenchymal cells into cranial bones and the generation of an adequate pool of stem/progenitor cells, thereby disrupting the patency of the developing suture via premature loss of stem/progenitor cells. Furthermore, investigators have identified Gli1+ cells as the predominant population of stem cells within the suture mesenchyme [3]. These cells give rise to the periosteum and dura and serve as the key stem cell population for mature craniofacial bones. Furthermore, deletion of this cell population has been shown to result in craniosynostosis, arrest of skull growth, and osteoporosis [3]. W ell known syndromes associated with craniosynostosis include Crouzon syndrome, Apert syndrome, Pfeiffer syndrome, Muenke syndrome, and Saethre-Chotzen syndrome [13]. These syndromes may all be either autosomal-dominant or sporadic (a newly arisen mutation) in their inheritance, and affect genes such as FGFR1-3, and TWIST1 [13]. In fact, out of 474 unique patients, a total of 64 mutations of six different genes were identified [14]. The six genes identified were MSX2, FGFR1 , FGFR3, FGFR2 , FBN1, and TWIST. W hile most FGFR mutations are identified as missense mutations, most TWIST gene mutations were noted to be nonsense changes or base pair duplications [14]. Compared with syndromic craniosynostosis, non-syndromic craniosynostosis is less well- characterized, even though it accounts for the majority of craniosynostosis cases [15, 16]. C raniosynostosis can lead to a myriad of deleterious conditions to the developing infant. Although each syndrome is unique, they can share similar craniofacial characteristics, such as skull and midfacial malformations, wide-set and/or bulging eyes, and/or a depressed nasal bridge [17]. Unfortunately, there are several comorbidities that often arise with syndromic craniosynostosis, such as obstructive sleep apnea, airway compromise, incomplete eyelid closure, hearing loss, difficulties with speech development, vision deficiency, limb/hand deformities, and rarely intellectual or developmental disabilities [17-19]. While most of these complications are more commonly associated with more severe and syndromic forms of craniosynostosis, patients with non- syndromic craniosynostosis can also present with these medical conditions. The most dangerous comorbidity of craniosynostosis is an elevation in intracranial pressure which can occur even in single-suture craniosynostosis patients without a genetic diagnosis, which carries implications for hindering proper brain development [20]. Langer and Vacanti cite Skalak and Fox, who described tissue engineering as a discipline that lies at the intersection of science and medicine, and ultimately aims to generate functional tissues in vivo as a means of treating various diseases [25-27]. There are several tissue engineering approaches that ultimately aim to restore normal biological function. The first approach involves purely the engineering and replacement of affected cell populations with subsequent replacement. The second strategy involves the delivery of substances, such as growth factors, which aim to induce tissue formation. DENTINOGENESIS IMPERFECTA: HISTORY , CLINICAL FEATURES, CLASSIFICATIONS, MECHANISMS, AND MANAGEMENT Xin Wang, Tian Liang AB STRACT D entinogenesis imperfecta (DGI) is the most common inherited dentin disorder. Patients with DGI show dental defects including tooth discoloration, attrition, bulbous crown, pulp obliteration, and “shell teeth”. Shields proposed a classiﬁcation system with three types of DGI and two types of dentin dysplasia (DD) for hereditary dentin defects. With advancements in molecular genetics, researchers have found that non- syndromic DGI/DD (excluding DD-I) is exclusively caused by DSPP mutations. Findings in dental and genetic defects in DGI patients and molecular mechanisms in mouse models carrying human DSPP mutations indicate that 5’ and 3’ DSPP mutations cause diﬀerent types of DGI via distinct pathological mechanisms. Particularly, 5’ DSPP mutations cause both dentin and enamel defects, potentially due to endoplasmic reticulum stress in dentin- and enamel

diﬀerent types of DGI via distinct pathological mechanisms. Particularly, 5’ DSPP mutations cause both dentin and enamel defects, potentially due to endoplasmic reticulum stress in dentin- and enamel -forming cells. 3’ DSPP mutations cause severe dentin defects because of strong autophagy activities in dentin -forming cells. These insights facilitate the proposal of a revised Shields’ classiﬁcation and are critical for the development of molecular therapies that can precisely treat DGI according to the molecular mechanisms. Currently, multidisciplinary treatments are necessary for the management of DGI patients. Early interventions are preferred. In terms of orthodontic treatments, both ﬁxed appliances and clear aligners have been used, although evidence on outcomes remains limited. Clinicians should take the weakened dental hard tissues into consideration when performing treatment planning. MOLECULAR MECHANISMS With advancements in molecular biology technologies, the gene encoding dentin sialophosphoprotein (DSPP) was identiﬁed [12] and associated with DGI [13, 14]. Cumulative evidence indicates that DD-II, DGI- II, and DGI -III are exclusively caused by DSPP mutations. Mutations in genes causing osteogenesis imperfecta, including COL1A1 and COL1A2 that encode procollagen chains of type I collagen, may lead to DGI-I [15, 16]. Several genes have been associated with DD-I [17], although there is still ambiguity in associations of clinical features and genetic discoveries. By far, there have been more than 50 DSPP mutations that cause DD-II, DGI-II, and DGI-III reported in the literature [11, 18, 19] . These mutations can be primarily divided into two categories: 1) 5’ DSPP mutations, mostly missense or intronic mutations that will alter the amino acid sequence around the signal peptide cleavage site or the N -terminal targeting region, and 2) 3’ DSPP mutations, all of

P mutations, mostly missense or intronic mutations that will alter the amino acid sequence around the signal peptide cleavage site or the N -terminal targeting region, and 2) 3’ DSPP mutations, all of which are -1 frameshift (-1fs) mutations that change the hydrophilic DPP into hydrophobic mutant proteins [11]. There seems to be a correlation between DSPP mutations and DGI phenotypes, potentially via distinct molecular mechanisms. DSPP is predominantly expressed by odontoblasts (dentin-forming cells) and transiently expressed by ameloblasts (enamel-forming cells) [20, 21]. The two major DSPP cleavage products, dentin sialoprotein (DSP) and dentin phosphoprotein (DPP), were discovered long before the identiﬁcation of DSPP gene, because of their unique biochemical properties [22, 23]. DPP is the most acidic protein in humans with an isoelectric point of 1.1 [24]. DSP is a glycoprotein [23, 25]. Proteoglycan forms of DSP are also identiﬁed [26-29]. The acidity of DPP and the carbohydrate units on DSP may be essential for dentin mineralization. Mice without DSP and DPP develop limited mineralized dentin: large areas of the dentin matrix remain unmineralized as predentin [21, 30]. Mice without DPP show hypomineralized dentin globules [21, 31]. Neither mouse shows dentin defects in heterozygous conditions. Dental pulps of mice without DSP and/or DPP do not get obliterated over time [30, 32]. The molecular pathological mechanisms of DGI have been further explored using DsppP19L and Dspp- 1fs mice [36]. In both types of mice, DSPP proteins accumulate in odontoblasts and ameloblasts. In DsppP19L mice, DSPP proteins are retained in ameloblasts for a longer duration, likely causing cellular stress that impacts enamel mineralization. The secretion of DSPP is also impaired in odontoblasts of DsppP19L mice, with most DSPP proteins remaining in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) that cause ER stress [33, 36] . Although DSPP proteins also accumulate in the ameloblasts of Dspp-1fs mice, the cellular retention of DSPP proteins is relatively brief, causing minimal enamel defects, if any, in Dspp-1fs mice [33, 36]. When the repetitive acidic normal DPP is mutated into a hydrophobic mutant protein in Dspp-1fs mice, strong autophagy activities are detected in odontoblasts of Dspp-1fs mice, leading to severe dentin defects. Therefore, a revised Shields’ classiﬁcation has been proposed based on genetic mutations [11]. First, 5’ DSPP mutations usually lead to both enamel and dentin developmental defects. The enamel and dentin defects are most likely caused by ER stress in ameloblasts and odontoblasts. Since DGI -III patients from the Brandywine isolate carry a 5’ DSPP mutation, it is logical to assign the diagnosis of DGI -III to patients carrying 5’ DSPP mutations. Second, dentin defects caused by 3’ DSPP mutations show variability in severity [11, 41]. Thus, patients with more severe dentin defects caused by 3’ DSPP mutations should be diagnosed as DGI -II, whereas those with milder dentin defects due to 3’ DSPP mutations should be considered DD-II (Table 1). Currently, patients with DGI often require comprehensive multidisciplinary care involving pediatric dentistry, endodontics, periodontics, prosthodontics, and orthodontics. The primary goals are to preserve functions of teeth, to ensure satisfactory esthetics and phonetics, and to support long-term oral health. Ideally, intervention should begin before or around the time of full eruption of the primary dentition to prevent excessive wear and maintain occlusal development [43]. SUMMARY D GI is the most common inherited dentin disorder. Except for DD -I, which is characterized by short roots, non-syndromic DGI is exclusively caused by DSPP mutations that can be primarily categorized into two types: 5’ and 3’ DSPP mutations. Findings in both human patients with DGI and mouse models carrying human DSPP mutations indicate that the dental defects resulting from these two types of DSPP mutations and the molecular mechanisms underlying these two types of DSPP mutations are distinct. These ﬁndings facilitate the diﬀerential diagnosis and the development of precise molecular therapeutic options based on DSPP mutations. Accurate segmentation of teeth in CBCT scans is essential for modern dental diagnostics, as it enables the early detection and precise assessment of various dental anomalies [2]. Tooth agenesis, a condition characterized by the congenital absence of one or more teeth, can significantly impact both primary an d permanent dentition, often requiring early intervention to prevent malocclusion and guide proper jaw development [3, 4]. S imilarly, eruption path deviations , such as impacted or ectopically erupting teeth , pose challenges in pediatric dentistry, as they can disrupt the alignment of adjacent teeth and lead to complications like crowding or impaction [5, 6]. CBCT segmentation provides a clear three- dimensional (3D) visualization of these abnormalities, allowing clinicians to predict eruption patterns and plan corrective measures [7]. By isolating individual teeth and their surrounding structures, segmentation helps monitor subtle changes in root morphology, enabling timely diagnosis and intervention to preserve tooth integrity [9-11]. These applications are especially vital in pediatric patients, where early detection and management of such conditions can significantly improve long - term oral health outcomes. Segmentation was performed by specialists using computer-based tools to accurately trace anatomical contours in axial slices, ensuring both anatomical fidelity and spatial consistency across segments. This study thus represents a fundamental milestone in the history of manual segmentation, serving as a foundation for the development of hybrid and automated techniques in the following decades. M anual segmentation, considered the most direct method for segmenting medical images, involves tracing anatomical structures in each image slice. By defining a region of interest (ROI) in each section, it is possible to construct a volume of interest through the sequential merging of these delineated regions. This approach proves particularly valuable in complex scenarios, such as those involving low-resolution images, the presence of artifacts, or intricate anatomical morphologies. By providing precise delineations in two-dimensional (2D) or 3D images, manual segmentation enables not only the 3D reconstruction of anatomical structures but also the volumetric measurement of relevant tissues [15]. Two experienced clinicians performed repeated manual segmentations, with a minimum interval of two weeks between sessions. The resulting average variation ranged from 2.5% to 3.5%, demonstrating high reproducibility and no statistically significant difference between operators [16]. However, despite its reliability, manual segmentation is extremely time-consuming and heavily dependent on the operator's skill. Consequently, although highly accurate, its routine application remains limited. In light of these constraints, alternative approaches have been explored to optimize the balance between accuracy and processing time, to enhance the clinical feasibility of segmentation. A nn-U-Net deep learning framework , a semantic segmentation method based on deep neural networks, specifically developed for applications in medical imaging, was employed for dental arch segmentation. It employs an architecture inspired by the conventional U-Net, with the key advantage of automatically adapting to new tasks without requiring any manual intervention from the user. This approach automates the entire segmentation pipeline, including preprocessing, network architecture definition, training parameter configuration, and post -processing. The automation process is guided by three types of parameters: fixed (based on established best practices), rule -based (derived from dataset-specific characteristics), and empirical (adjusted during training) [49]. CONCLUSIONS T he progressive integration of AI into dental imaging has transformed the segmentation of dento- maxillofacial structures, particularly in CBCT. This chapter demonstrated the evolution from labor - intensive manual segmentation methods to increasingly robust and efficient automated techniques, emphasizing their application in pediatric patients with developing dentitions. While manual and semi-automatic methods remain essential for validation and refinement, deep learning -based segmentation models , such as Ped iatricDentalSegmentator, have shown high accuracy and consistency. These tools not only reduce segmentation time dramatically but also improve accessibility through open-source deployment, addressing critical needs in both research and clinical contexts. N C left lip and/or palate (CLP) are the most common craniofacial anomalies, resulting from a failure in the fusion of facial prominences during early embryogenesis [1]. The global incidence of CLP is estimated at approximately 1.7 per 1,000 live births, with notable geographic variation [2] . The etiology of CLP is multifactorial, involving a combination of genetic and environmental factors [3-5]. Complete clefts extend through the lip, alveolus, and palate, while incomplete clefts may involve only a subset of these structures. CLP can also be c lassified as unilateral or bilateral and may occur in isolation (non -syndromic) or as part of a syndrome (syndromic) [6]. The presence of an alveolar cleft disrupts the continuity of the maxillary arch, affecting dental development and craniofacial growth. Teeth adjacent to the cleft —particularly the lateral incisor and canine—often present with abnormal positioning or impact ion due to the lack of bon y support [7]. This discontinuity also compromises masticatory function, nasal floor integrity, and midfacial development , leading to malocclusion, transverse maxillary collapse, and facial asymmetry. Additionally, the persistence of an oronasal fistula may impair speech and nasal airflow, further complicating rehabilitation [8]. Effective management of CLP requires a multidisciplinary approach, integrating the expertise of plastic surgeons, oral and maxillofacial surgeons, orthodontists, speech -language pathologists, psychologists, and other professionals [9]. Secondary alveolar bone grafting (SABG) is performed during the mixed dentition stage (9–12 years), prior to the eruption of the permanent canine [ 10-12]; furthermore, other protocols and timings may also be applied achieving the success [13]. ABG provides maxillary stabilization, closure of oronasal fistulas, nasal base support, periodontal health, and facilitates orthodontic and prosthetic rehabilitation [7, 14]. T he iliac crest has traditionally been the gold standard donor site due to its abundant cancellous bone. However, it is associated with donor site morbidity, including postoperative pain, gait disturbances, and non-aesthetic scar [15]. In contrast, the mandibular symphysis has emerged as an alternative donor site due to its proximity, ease of access, and lower morbidity. Studies have

, gait disturbances, and non-aesthetic scar [15]. In contrast, the mandibular symphysis has emerged as an alternative donor site due to its proximity, ease of access, and lower morbidity. Studies have reported comparable success rates between mandibular symphysis and iliac crest bone in achieving bone formation [15-26] and supporting spontaneous tooth eruption through the grafted area [21, 27]. The symphyseal approach is performed intraorally, avoiding external scars, and provides sufficient bone for unilateral clefts [15-26]. T he evaluation of ABG outcomes has significantly advanced with the use of cone beam computed tomography (CBCT), which enables comprehensive three-dimensional (3D) visualization of the cleft area, and the bone bridge formed in the alveolus . CBCT enables high -resolution analysis, allowing precise quantification of bone formation and measurement of buccopalatal and vertical dimensions of the new bone bridge —overcoming the limitations of conventional two

h -resolution analysis, allowing precise quantification of bone formation and measurement of buccopalatal and vertical dimensions of the new bone bridge —overcoming the limitations of conventional two -dimensional (2D) imaging, which often underestimates graft outcomes due to projection distortion and anatomical overlap [ 25, 28, 29]. When enhanced with artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools, CBCT further improves reproducibility and enables automated, detailed evaluations of graft success [30]. This pilot study aimed to assess ABG outcomes using mandibular symphysis bone and to investigate donor site healing dynamics through a novel AI - enhanced 3D assessment protocol. DISCUSSION T he integration of CBCT with AI -based tools has significantly advanced the evaluation of ABG outcomes. Unlike conventional 2D radiographs—limited by projection distortions and lack of volumetric detail [12, 25, 28, 33]—CBCT provides high -resolution 3D data. When enhanced by AI -driven segmentation, this approach improves the efficiency, reproducibility, and

distortions and lack of volumetric detail [12, 25, 28, 33]—CBCT provides high -resolution 3D data. When enhanced by AI -driven segmentation, this approach improves the efficiency, reproducibility, and objectivity of volumetric assessments, achieving a level of precision comparable to that of expert clinicians [34]. Preliminary CBCT analysis of this subsample revealed consistent reductions in cleft width postoperatively, with near- zero values at the apical level—indicating not only successful graft integration but also the sensitivity of this AI integrated methodology to detect subtle morphological changes. Notably, the individualized segmentation of anatomical structures enabled accurate measurements even in cases with teeth in the cleft region. The variability observed in pre - and postoperative cleft dimensions re flects the inherent anatomical heterogeneity of cleft morphology [35, 36], rather than methodological inconsistencies. This individualized, image -guided analysis can

This individualized, image -guided analysis can support more precise clinical decision- making and may contribute to optimized treatment strategies, potentially improving outcomes and long-term care for each patient. Th e preliminary ABG outcomes support the effectiveness of mandibular symphysis bone as a reliable graft source for cleft reconstruction. The reconstructed alveolar ridge demonstrated notable buccopalatal thickness, mesiodistal extension, and vertical height—parameters considered essential for functional and anatomical success [12, 13, 21, 25, 26, 31]. Despite the symphyseal region offering smaller graft volumes compared to the iliac crest, it was sufficient for achieving almost full defect closure in this cohort. Furthermore, harvesting from the mandibular symphysis results in less morbidity, faster recovery, and shorter hospitalization periods when compared to extraoral donor sites [37]. M oreover, the presence of a robust and continuous bone bridge plays a central role in the multidisciplinary rehabilitation of patients with CLP . Grafted alveolar ridges serve as a foundation for future prosthodontic interventions, including dental implants, which demonstrate success rates comparable to those placed in non- cleft patients [ 38, 39]. Additionally, a stable bone union across the cleft facilitates favorable conditions for orthognathic surgery, often allowing for one -piece LeFort I Mandibular Symphysis Bone for Alveolar Bone Grafting Ribeiro Braga et al. 154

advancements and avoiding the need for multi -segment osteotomies, which are more invasive and less stable [29]. Thus, the bone morphology achieved in this study not only fulfilled immediate reconstructive goals but may also lay the groundwork for long-term functional and esthetic rehabilitation. H ealing at the mandibular symphysis donor site was favorable, with no adverse clinical outcomes. Although concerns have been raised regarding potential effects on mandibular growth, facial contour, and future genioplasty, current longitudinal evidence indi cates that symphyseal bone harvesting does not significantly impact mandibular development or chin projection [24, 40]. When present, minor contour alterations are transient and fall within the range of normal physiological remodeling [4 0]. Donor site morbidity remains low, with minimal neurosensory disturbance and preserved vitality of adjacent teeth [41-43]. Donor site morbidity remains low, with minimal neurosensory disturbance and preserved vitality of adjacent teeth [41-43]. In this cohort, the residual bone was minimal (2.7 ± 1.4 mm), and no cases of pulpal or sensory impairment were noted, reinforcing the symphyseal region as a probable safe and reliable autogenous donor site for alveolar cleft reconstruction. T his p reliminary study, which is part of an ongoing clinical investigation, confirmed the methodological feasibility of using mandibular symphysis bone for alveolar cleft reconstruction. Despite the small sample size, the use of a standardized surgical protocol, consistent execution by a single experienced surgeon, and the integration of AI-enhanced 3D imaging analysis provided a solid framework for assessing outcomes related both to alveolar bone formation and regeneration at the donor site. The anatomical and functional results observed may support the reliability of the mandibular symphysis as a donor site for ABG, demonstrating favorable graft integration and low morbidity. These preliminary findings support the viability of the proposed methodology and justify its continued application in subsequent phases of the trial, which will incorporate comparative groups involving alternative autogenous graft sources and adjunctive biomaterials. CONCLUSIONS C BCT-based 3D analyses enhanced by AI-powered tools provided a precise and consistent approach for assessing graft formation and donor- site regeneration. The notable bone bridge formation supports the mandibular symphysis as a viable donor site for ABG in patients with unilateral CLP, justifying its continued assessment and validation of reproducibility in the larger cohort of this ongoing RCT. Forty-nine children aged between 7 and 11 years with AOB were prospectively and randomly allocated in either the experimental group (24 patients treated with bonded spurs associated with build-ups, 17 female, 7 male; mean age of 8.22+1.06 years) or the comparison group (25 patients treated with bonded spurs, 14 female; 11 male; mean age of 8.30+ 0.99 years). Both protocols were demonstrated to be effective in early treatment of AOB, without significant differences. KEY WORDS: Open bite, Orthodontic appliance, Bonded spurs INTRODUCTION Anterior open bite (AOB) is defined by the absence of vertical contact between the upper and lower incisors while posterior teeth remain in occlusion [1, 2]. AOB is considered one of the most challenging malocclusions to treat in the permanent dentition, as the treatment often involves more complex and less stable orthodontic interventions [1, 2]. This vertical discrepancy can lead to functional problems, such as difficulties in incising food and pronouncing certain phonemes [3 -5]. In addition, AOB can lead to esthetic concerns affecting the facial profile and the smile [3-5]. As a result, patients with AOB may experience psychosocial issues, including socialization difficulties, which can negatively affect their quality of life [3 -5]. Therefore, early inter vention of AOB offers several advantages, such as preventing the establishment of deleterious habits, promoting normal dentoalveolar development, reducing the need for more invasive procedures in the future, and improving the patient’s self-esteem and overall quality of life during growth and development [6, 7]. Th e prevalence of AOB in the mixed dentition is 17% [8, 9]. The etiology of AOB is considered multifactorial, involving genetic and environmental factors [1, 9, 10]. Deleterious oral habits, such as pacifier or thumb sucking, tongue thrusting, and mouth breathing represent the most common environmental factors associated with AOB [9, 10]. The establishment of AOB depends not only on the presence of deleterious oral habits, but also on their frequency, duration, and intensity, as described by Graber’s triad [11]. This association is so strong that both prolonged sucking habits and hyperdivergent vertical skeletal relationships significantly increased the probability of developing AOB, with prevalence rates reaching up to 36.3% [9]. W hen the malocclusion is caused by deleterious habits, it is classified as dentoalveolar AOB, which generally has a good treatment prognosis if the causal factors are eliminated [1, 9, 10, 12]. Even bone tissue, despite being structurally strong, can become malleable when subject to prolonged and low-intensity forces, inhibiting incisors’ dentoalveolar vertical development and resulting in AOB [11]. On the other hand, when AOB is related to genetic factors, it is classified as skeletal AOB [12]. These features predispose to an increased gonial angle, generating clockwise mandibular rotation and an increase in lower anterior facial height [2, 10, 13]. The greater the influence of genetic factors, the poorer the treatment prognosis [2, 10, 13]. The gold standard for treating dentoalveolar AOB in the mixed dentition is the fixed palatal crib [16 -20]. This device acts as a mechanical barrier, preventing the execution of deleterious oral habits, promoting the vertical development of the incisors, and consequently correcting the dentoalveolar AOB [16-21]. The palatal crib can be fixed or removable, but the main disadvantage of removable appliances is the need for patient compliance to achieve successful outcomes [17]. Therefore, the fixed appliance is generally preferred [16]. Furthermore, the muscular imbalance between intraoral and perioral musculature caused by deleterious oral habits can lead to transverse discrepancy, such as posterior crossbite [27]. Bo nded spurs placed in the palatal and lingual surfaces of upper and lower incisors, respectively, can be considered an effective alternative for early treatment of AOB [14, 15, 17, 18, 22, 24, 25]. A OB is often associated with a vertical growth pattern and increased anterior facial height [2, 9, 10]. If left untreated, this relationship may worsen with age, leading to more severe malocclusion [10, 29, 30]. Therefore, a question arises: could combining bonded spurs with posterior build-ups on the upper deciduous and first permanent molars potentially enhance AOB correction compared to bonded spurs alone in the mixed dentition? METHODS To evaluate this hypothesis, a randomized clinical trial was conducted at Bauru Dental School, University of São Paulo, to compare the changes produced by bonded spurs combined with posterior build-ups versus conventional bonded spurs in the early treatmen t of AOB [32 -36]. The study was approved by the Ethics in Research Committee of this institution, and informed consent was obtained from all patients and their parents or legal guardians. The inclusion criteria were: patients aged between 7 and 11 years, AOB > 1 mm (clinically evaluated as the vertical distance between the incisal edges of the maxillary and mandibular central incisors), erupted first permanent molars, with the maxillary and mandibular permanent central incisors fully erupted, without or with only mild crowding, and without the need for maxillary expansion. ESTHETIC ALTERNATIVE FOR ANTERIOR OPEN BITE TREATMENT IN THE MIXED DENTITION Camila Massaro, Gabriela Utrago, Amanda Marques, Lourival Garcia, Aron Aliaga-del Castillo, Lucia Cevidanes, Daniela Garib ABSTRACT Anterior open bite (AOB) is a malocclusion characterized by the lack of vertical overlap between the upper and lower incisors when the posterior teeth are in contact. It can affect masticatory function, speech, and smile esthetics, influencing the child’s self- perception and social integration. Early treatment during the mixed dentition phase is recommended with the potential of improving the quality of life of patients. Among the therapeutic options for early AOB intervention, removable appliances such as the high -pull chin cup and removable palatal crib are used, but their success depends on patient compliance. success depends on patient compliance. The fixed palatal crib is widely recognized as the gold standard for interceptive treatment of AOB, effectively promoting bite closure by mechanically preventing tongue thrust and discouraging habi ts like thumb sucking. This chapter introduces the Esthetic Palatal Crib (Ice Crib), an innovative fixed appliance that combines the classic metallic palatal structure with transparent extensions in the anterior region , enhancing esthetic and social accept ance without compromising therapeutic effectiveness. Preliminary results show promising outcomes in AOB closure and habit cessation with the Esthetic Palatal Crib. In addition, good acceptance was reported by the first patients to receive the appliance. Further studies will continue to evaluate the clinical outcomes of the Esthetic Palatal Crib, aiming to support its integration into orthodontic practice. KEY WORDS: Interceptive orthodontics, Orthodontic a ppliance design, Anterior open bite, Esthetic Palatal Crib INTRODUCTION I nterceptive orthodontic treatment can benefit the patient’s developmen t. W hen properly indicated, interceptive orthodontic treatment may simplify or even eliminate the need for a second intervention [1, 2]. In this context, anterior open bite (AOB) deserves our attention. This malocclusion is defined by the lack of vertical contact between anterior teeth, while the posterior teeth are in occlusion, resulting in a negative overbite [3, 4]. The negative impact of this condition on children’s quality of life [5], as well as the prove n benefit of early treatment when indicated [6, 7], make this topic of great relevance in orthodontics. A comprehensive understanding of the etiology and clinical characteristics of AOB is essential for accurate diagnosis, appropriate selection of a suitable therapeutic intervention, and determination of the ideal timing for treatment. The etiology of AOB is considered multifactorial, and may be related to genetic factors, environmental influences, or a combination of both [3, 8] . The persistence of deleterious oral habits, such as thumb or pacifier sucking and tongue thrusting, is a major etiological factor in this condition [3, 8]. When the AOB is primarily caused by persistent non -nutritive sucking habits, it generally presents a dentoalveolar pattern with a favorable treatment prognosis and post - treatment stability, if the etiological factor is removed [8]. In contrast, when the etiology is skeletal and genetically determined, the condition tends to be more complex and less pred ictable [3].

Additionally, airway obstruction and mouth breathing must be considered during the etiological investigation of AOB [3]. In such cases, referral to an otolaryngologist should precede orthodontic intervention. I n the deciduous dentition, t he prevalence of AOB is approximately 27% among children with non-nutritive sucking habits [9]. In the mixed dentition, AOB affects approximately 18% of children [8, 10, 11] . In the presence of non-nutritive sucking habits and /or a vertical growth pattern, this prevalence increases to 36.3% [8]. The decrease in the prevalence of AOB from deciduous to mixed dentition phase can be explained by the spontaneous correction of the overbite after the abandonment of such habits [12]. P revious studies showed that AOB can affect not only masticatory and speech function but also smile esthetics, influencing self-perception and potentially impacting social integration and quality of life [13, 14] . The interceptive treatment of AOB plays a critical role by helping to eliminate persistent deleterious oral habits, correct tongue posture, guide proper tooth positioning, and support normal dental development [16]. These measures not only improve function and esthetics but also contribute to the long- term stability of treatment outcomes [16-20]. A variety of options are available for AOB treatment, including fixed palatal crib, bonded spurs, high-pull chin cup, and removable palatal crib [18]. The fixed palatal crib (Figure 1) is a classic device traditionally used in the management of deleterious oral habits in orthodontics. First described in the mid-1940s, [21, 22] it remains the gold standard to this day. Figure 1. Fixed palatal crib. A) Frontal View, B) Occlusal view. Although the design of the fixed palatal crib remains similar today, the gold wire has been replaced with stainless steel, offering greater durability and cost- effectiveness. The design of the appliance can be modified in the presence of transverse discrepancies [17, 19]. In individuals with non -nutritive sucking habits, such as pacifier or thumb sucking, the tongue often remains in low position and may be unable to apply the necessary pressure against the palate for transverse maxillary arch growth [24, 25]. Moreover, in an attempt to achieve an anterior seal, which is compromised due to the presence of a negative overbite, the tongue tends to adopt an abnormal posture at rest and during swallowing [16]. This dysfunctional posture impairs normal tongue function and may also contribute to the development or persistence of transverse discrepancies [24, 25] . Therefore, the use of a Q uad-Helix appliance in combination with palatal crib represents a viable treatment option in such cases, as it addresses both the vertical and transversal discrepancies [17, 19]. The fixed palatal crib is a passive device [16, 23], which acts as a mechanical barrier, preventing the persistence of deleterious oral habits [16, 23]. As a result, the anterior teeth undergo extrusion along with the alveolar process until a positive overbite is passively achieved [16, 17, 19, 20, 26, 27]. In addition to the vertical changes, the maxillary and mandibular incisors exhibit lingual tipping, contributing to relative extrusion that further facilitates AOB closure [16, 17, 19, 20, 27]. ndibular incisors exhibit lingual tipping, contributing to relative extrusion that further facilitates AOB closure [16, 17, 19, 20, 27]. Several studies have demonstrated favorable long-term stability after AOB correction with fixed palatal cribs during the mixed dentition [16-20]. Reported stability rates ranged from 80% to 100% in treatment performed during the mixed dentition [16-20]. In contrast, stability rates in the permanent dentition are lower, ranging from 62% to 75%, and typically required more complex interventions [28, 29]. The greater stability observed in early treatment may be attributed to the elimination of deleterious oral habits that act as mechanical barriers to vertical development of anterior teeth [16- 20]. These findings support the clinical effectiveness of fixed palatal cribs in allowing anterior vertical development of incisors and in disrupting harmful habits, contributing to long-term stability [16-20]. Bonded spurs are also indicated for the early treatment of AOB [7, 18, 26, 27] . This alternative offers some advantages, including low cost, improved esthetics, elimination of the laboratory phase, a simplified technique, and reduced chair time [18, 27]. Bonded spurs are attached to the lingual surfaces of the incisors rather than supported by molar bands, as seen with fixed palatal cribs [7, 26]. Despite the benefits, bonded spurs tend to be less effective in correcting AOB [27] and in eliminating persistent oral habits [18]. Additionally, bonded spurs demonstrated some disadvantages such as frequent debonding during treatment [27]. In children, especially in those with persistent sucking habits, fixed appliances are generally preferred, as they do not rely on patient cooperation. Currently, there is increasing demand for more esthetic and discreet orthodontic appliances [30]. Esthetic concerns during interceptive orthodontic treatment should also be considered, as many patients may face bullying, embarrassment, or negative comments in the school environment [13, 30]. This intervention should be coordinated within an interdisciplinary team and involve the selection of the most effective appliance to promote AOB closure. The fixed palatal crib remains the gold standard for early treatment in this stage. The dental anomalies , ranging from malocclusion to alterations in dental arch form, combined with maxillofacial discrepancies, impose complex demands not routinely encountered in conventional orthodontics. In many cases, comprehensive care extends from the early mixed dentition period through to post -surgical rehabilitation, necessitating an orthodontic assessment tool that can capture both gross occlusal discrepancies and subtle reﬁnements following therapy [1]. Data were collected from 31 nonsyndromic UCLP patients who received comprehensive orthodontic treatment at a high-volume cleft center in Brazil. Patients were selected based on strict inclusion criteria, namely the availability of high- resolution pre -treatment and post -treatment digital dental models along with corresponding panoramic radiographs. The treatments were uniformly performed using conventional ﬁxed-appliance therapy, ensuring consistency in the treatment approach across the sample. Th e COR Scoring Grid A t the core of the COR system is a structured scoring grid that systematically evaluates a set of occlusal parameters (Table 1). The system focuses on static occlusion and includes: anteroposterior relationship assessed separately in the anterior and posterior segments; vertical relationship based on the presence or extent of positive/negative overbite or open bite in the anterior and posterior regions; transverse relationship evaluating edge-to-edge or buccal/lingual crossbites, weighted by severity and number of aﬀected teeth; alignment assessed

Each row of the grid corresponds to a particular occlusal characteristic. Parameters are scored on a scale from 0 to 4, with 0 indicating no deviation from ideal occlusion and 4 reﬂecting the most severe anomaly. DISCUSSION The present study aimed to evaluate the predictability of tooth movements and arch form changes achieved with clear aligner therapy in a cohort of patients CLP . This patient population presents unique challenges due to inherent skeletal and dental characteristics, arch form alteration, and potential growth disturbances. Understanding the efficacy of clear aligners in these complex patients is crucial for optimizing treatment strategies and managing patient expectations [2, 9] . predictability of individual tooth movements reveal that, similar to non -cleft populations, clear aligners exhibit limitations in achieving certain prescribed movements with complete accuracy in CLP patients. The LC was statistically significant for a majority of movements across various tooth types when compared to clinically relevant thresholds (0.5 mm for translations, 2° for rotations). This aligns with the broader literature on clear aligner efficacy [6], which consistently reports discrepancies between planned and achieved outcomes . Specifically, lateral incisors demonstrated significant LC across most of the movement. This is a particularly relevant finding in CLP patients, as lateral incisors are frequently affected by the cleft, often being congenitally missing, peg -shaped, or malpositioned [24]. The proximity to the cleft can make them challenging to move predictably with any orthodontic appliance, and our results suggest clear aligners are no exception. The high LC for

The high LC for torque and rotation of canines and premolars also aligns with findings in non-cleft samples [10-12], suggesting that the biomechanical limitations of applying rotational and torquing forces with aligners persist in the CLP context. Interestingly, torque correction for central incisors is a highly predictable movement. This can be explained considering that most of the prescribed torque was to reduce torque; this is a predictable movement as shown by Wei and coworker [17]. The observation that the amount of prescribed movement (PM) was a significant predictor of LC is consistent with previous research [10]. Larger prescribed movements tend to result in a greater absolute lack of correction, emphasizing the need for careful staging of movements and potential overcorrection in the virtual setup, especially for movements known to be less predictable. The results of this study have several clinical implications for the orthodontic management of CLP patients with clear aligners. Clinicians should be aware of the movements that are less predictable (e.g., torque and rotation of canines and incisors, especially compromised lateral incisors) and incorporate appropriate overcorrections or plan for adjunctive techniques or refinements. The ability of clear aligners to effect changes in both symmetric and asymmetric aspects of arch form is promising. Expansion with retraction is a highly predictable movement. However, the incomplete achievement of planned outcomes suggests that for significant transverse discrepancies or asymmetries, aligners alone might be insufficient, or may require more extensive overcorrection and adjunctive therapies (e.g., miniscrew). This study has limitations. Its retrospective nature is one. Although a single experienced clinician treated all patients, variations in individual patient response and compliance

s (e.g., miniscrew). This study has limitations. Its retrospective nature is one. Although a single experienced clinician treated all patients, variations in individual patient response and compliance could influence outcomes. The sample represents a specific treatment protoco l and aligner system; results might differ with other systems or protocols (e.g., different attachment strategies, aligner change intervals). The methodology used for superimposition has been validated in the literature, but the lack of fixed external reference points still decreases the reliability of the measurements. Future research should focus on prospective studies to further validate these findings and explore the influence of specific CLP characteristics (e.g., cleft type, severity, previous orthopedic treatment ) on aligner treatment predictability. Investigating the efficacy of different auxiliaries, like hybrid therapy or miniscrew, could lead to improved clinical protocols. Longitudinal studies

Longitudinal studies assessing the stability of clear aligner outcomes in this population are also needed. CONCLUSIONS Clear aligner therapy can induce significant tooth movements and changes in maxillary arch form in patients with cleft lip and palate. However, similar to observations in non-cleft populations, discrepancies exist between planned and achieved outcomes. Cli nicians should consider these predictability patterns when planning treatments for patients with CLP, incorporating necessary overcorrections and anticipating the potential need for refinements or the use of auxiliaries to achieve optimal results.
